tier_reason: First-party numbers only: bench.sh (public, names i7-6700K and i7-1370P) times pf against procps pgrep, and the README footnote times pd against /bin/ps ax, but neither states the Nim/C compiler versions, the flags actually used for the benchmarked binaries, or the procps version and build, and the README ps timings name no machine; that falls short of A, and there is no independent measurement.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README footnote: pd -f%p %c 2.8576 ms +- 0.0070 vs /bin/ps ax 5.0281 ms +- 0.0063 (README says roughly 2X and 'about 57% the run-time'; 1.76x derived from page data); with process typology and highlights on, pd takes 3.9739 ms +- 0.0044, 1.27X faster than stock ps; pgrep and pkill are (5.025 +- 0.015)X and (5.745 +- 0.016)X slower than pf and pk for an 'average process' on a 4-core and a 20-core CPU. bench.sh comments (overhead subtracted): i7-6700K pf -e1 init 1014.1 us, pf -e1 with no match 2060.1 us, pgrep -x init 7724 us; i7-1370P 582.7 us, 1345.7 us and 5539.6 us; bench.sh calls this 'up to' 7.617x and 9.507x. The 'up to' figures compare pf stopping at the first /proc entry (init) with pgrep's full scan; the equal-work full-scan rows (pf with no match vs pgrep) give 3.75x and 4.12x (derived from page data), and the README 5.025X/5.745X figures are pgrep's time divided by the mean of pf's first-hit and no-match times (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: The gains come from doing less work, so this is a different, narrower program and not the same algorithm. pd -f%p %c reads only /proc/PID/stat and prints the pid and the 15-character comm. /bin/ps ax prints PID, TTY, STAT, TIME and the full argv (from /proc/PID/cmdline), and procps also parses /proc/PID/status, so the README ps comparison does not produce the same output. In bench.sh, -e1 means --exist --first (exit at the first match with no output). Because init is the first /proc entry, the 'up to 7.617x/9.507x' rows read one process while pgrep scans all of them; the equal-work no-match rows give 3.75x and 4.12x. procps pgrep 3.3.17 with a pattern sets PROC_FILLCOM and PROC_FILLSTATUS, so it reads cmdline and status for every process, while pf reads stat. The author says there are configurations where ps can be faster. The README timing machine and flags are unstated, the Nim/C compiler versions and the procps version are unstated, and bench.sh needs the author's tim and tails tools from c-blake/bu. These are millisecond-scale wins on a single-user tool. The nimble file says 'MIT/ISC' but LICENSE is ISC text.
corrections.why_faster: Fewer system calls and less parsing, not codegen. With a pid-and-command format, procs reads only /proc/PID/stat, while procps ps also opens and parses /proc/PID/status and /proc/PID/cmdline. procps pgrep with a pattern reads cmdline and status for every process (PROC_FILLCOM and PROC_FILLSTATUS in pgrep.c do_openproc), while pf matches on the stat comm field. pf -e1 also exits at the first match, while pgrep reads and selects every process before acting.

notes: Real first-party measurements, and the numbers match the README and bench.sh exactly. The win is a narrower program doing less /proc I/O, not the Nim language (language_level_claim false and same_algorithm false are correct; same_opt_level stays unknown because neither side's build flags are stated). The headline 'up to 7.6x/9.5x' pf-vs-pgrep figures compare early exit at the first process with a full scan (equal-work ratio is 3.75x/4.12x, derived), and the README ps comparison prints different columns. Record these as shortcomings. Metadata checked: ISC, 25 stars, 3 forks, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-07-04 (active).
